Among 1,582 critically ill infected patients (defined as infected patients with severe disease), the proportion falling into each immune dysregulation subgroup is:

1. System-wide dysregulation (both myeloid and lymphoid axes elevated): 66.8% (n=1,056)
2. Lymphoid dysregulation (selective lymphoid axis elevation): 19.1% (n=302)
3. Balanced (neither axis elevated): 7.5% (n=118)
4. Myeloid dysregulation (selective myeloid axis elevation): 6.7% (n=106)

System-wide dysregulation — concurrent innate and adaptive immune activation — is by far the dominant pattern, affecting two-thirds of critically ill sepsis patients. Lymphoid-predominant dysregulation accounts for nearly one-fifth, consistent with the immunosuppressive phase of sepsis. The balanced and myeloid-only subgroups are each under 8%, indicating that isolated dysregulation of a single immune axis is uncommon in severe disease.

These proportions are robust to the definition used: restricting to patients with explicit Severe or Fatal severity grades (n=1,374) yields nearly identical proportions (system-wide 65.6%, lymphoid 19.6%, balanced 8.0%, myeloid 6.8%). Among all infected patients (including non-severe), system-wide dysregulation drops to 45.3% and balanced rises to 25.4%, confirming that system-wide dysregulation is strongly enriched in critical illness.
